introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Question 6 b) : dates et exemples (London Docklands Development Corporation à partir de 1981, Canary Wharf, Albert Dock de Liverpool, Inner Harbor de Baltimore) reconnus.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) de trois sous-questions : codées « a », « b », « c » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b », « OR-c » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Sujet scanné de cinq pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de planche de carte topographique 1:50 000 « Dufftown » avec ses signes conventionnels, puis le fond de carte du Cameroun pour la question 3c i). Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2024, Three Hours. Filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés. La planche topographique (page 4) appartient aux épreuves de cartographie (Paper 3) et ne sert à aucune question de ce Paper 2 : non transcrite. Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 8+8+9, Q2 6+10+9, Q3 8+8+(3+6=9), Q4 6+10+9, Q5 5+9+11, Q6 8+9+8, Q7 EITHER 9+8+8, OR 6+10+9). Aucun écart avec le sujet. Le sujet imprime des marks pour un ensemble de sous-points (ex. Q1 a (i)+(ii) = 8 marks) : le corrigé les regroupe sous une seule sous-question.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Describe **THREE** ways by which technological changes or innovations over time have reduced the importance of the factors that influenced the location of early settlement.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Early settlements were located to meet basic needs: a **water supply** (springs, rivers, wells), **defence** (hilltops, river loops, islands), a **dry-point** site above floods and marsh, **fuel** (wood), **building materials**, shelter and **fertile land** and food close by, and, for towns, a route or crossing point. Technological change has made many of these needs less decisive (about 2.5 marks each).

**1. Water supply and drainage technology.** Pumps, boreholes, **piped water**, reservoirs and long-distance pipelines supply water to towns far from rivers and springs (for example Dubai, Las Vegas or Los Angeles). Embankments, dams, drainage and pumping make it possible to build on **flood plains and marshes**, and on reclaimed land (the Netherlands). The settlements no longer need a water-point or a dry-point site.

**2. Transport and energy.** Railways, roads, lorries, ships and aircraft bring in food, building materials and fuel from great distances, and **electricity, gas and oil** replaced firewood: a town no longer depends on the farmland, forest and quarries close by, and it can grow on a site chosen for other reasons (a port, a mining site, a political or industrial reason; for example Kribi or the new towns of the deserts). Refrigeration and storage allow the long-distance supply of food.

**3. Military technology, policing and construction methods.** With modern weapons and aircraft, hilltop and island **defensive sites** are no longer secure or necessary, and a settled national administration and police give security, so people leave the hill villages for the plains (as with the hill-top villages of the Mandara Mountains, where people have moved down to the plains). In addition, modern construction (reinforced concrete, steel, lifts and air-conditioning) and earth-moving machines enable people to build on steep, rocky, swampy or hot sites and in high-rise buildings, so that the choice of site depends less on shelter and building material.

(Other possible points: communication technology which lets people work at a distance, and irrigation and fertilisers which reduce the importance of local soil fertility.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Examine **THREE** ways of solving the problems of inner city decay.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Inner city decay** is the physical, economic and social decline of the older central areas of a city: old, overcrowded and run-down housing, derelict factories and warehouses, a loss of jobs, poverty and unemployment, poor services, crime and a poor environment, as people and firms move to the suburbs. Three ways of solving it are examined (3 marks each).

**1. Urban renewal and redevelopment of housing and land (physical regeneration).** Slum houses and derelict buildings are **cleared and rebuilt**, or **rehabilitated** (improved), with new or refurbished housing, open space and better services (water, sewers, lighting). A well-known example is the redevelopment of the **London Docklands** from 1981 by the London Docklands Development Corporation, which converted disused docks into offices (Canary Wharf), housing and leisure; others include the Albert Dock in Liverpool and Baltimore's Inner Harbor. *Evaluation:* it improves the environment and attracts investment, but the cost is high, and the original residents may be moved out by higher rents (gentrification).

**2. Economic regeneration: attracting investment and creating jobs.** Governments use **enterprise zones, tax incentives, grants and cheap land** to bring in new firms (offices, services, tourism, light industry and technology), train the unemployed, and encourage small businesses; the transport links are improved (for example the Docklands Light Railway) so that the area is connected to the rest of the city. *Evaluation:* it creates jobs, but the new jobs may go to commuters with better skills and not to local people, and it depends on the economy.

**3. Social and community-based measures, planning and participation.** Improving schools, health centres, policing and community facilities; helping local residents to take part in planning and in self-help improvement schemes (neighbourhood groups, housing associations, NGOs); controlling urban sprawl (green belts) and creating new or expanded towns, and encouraging people to return to live in the centre (mixed-use development, conversion of old buildings to flats). *Evaluation:* it is cheaper and lasting because the people support it, but the results come slowly.

**Conclusion:** the most successful schemes combine the physical, economic and social measures and involve the local community, so as to avoid pushing out the poor.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Describe **TWO** urban problems facing towns and cities in Cameroon today and explain how they can be remedied.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Cameroon's towns, especially Douala and Yaounde, have grown quickly (by rural-urban migration and natural increase) and often faster than the services and planning. Two problems are described, each with remedies (4 marks each).

**Problem 1: Housing shortage, slums and unplanned settlements.**
*Description:* many people live in overcrowded, poor-quality houses in **informal or spontaneous settlements** on the hillsides and swampy areas of the towns, without a title to the land, and with poor water supply, drains, electricity and roads; the sites are subject to flooding and landslides, and diseases (cholera, typhoid, malaria) spread easily.
*Remedies:* a **housing policy** with the state companies and agencies that provide land and houses (the Société Immobilière du Cameroun, the land agency MAETUR and the housing finance institution Crédit Foncier du Cameroun) and the government's social housing programme; **site-and-service schemes** and upgrading of existing slums (providing roads, water, drains and electricity instead of demolition); easier and cheaper **access to land titles and mortgages**; the enforcement of urban plans and building regulations; and the development of smaller towns and rural areas to reduce migration to the large cities.

**Problem 2: Waste disposal and poor sanitation (with flooding of blocked drains).**
*Description:* the quantity of household and market waste is greater than the capacity of the collection services, so that rubbish is dumped in streets, open spaces, streams and drains. **Blocked drains** cause floods and breeding places for mosquitoes, there is pollution of streams and wells, and a smell and disease risk.
*Remedies:* an **improved waste collection system** (more bins, trucks and collection points, and the use of the company in charge of urban cleaning, such as Hysacam, with the councils), sanitary **landfill sites**, composting and **recycling** (including of plastics), a ban on dumping and fines, **public education and neighbourhood clean-up campaigns**, and the building and cleaning of **drains and sewers**.

(Other problems that could be chosen: traffic congestion and the motorcycle taxis, unemployment and the informal sector, shortages of water and electricity, crime, and flooding.)
